title: Branches: a safe place to try ideas
objective: Learners follow a feature from branch to pull request, review and merge while a teammate ships an urgent fix to main, and see how merge, rebase and squash change the history and when a merge conflict happens.

recommended.why: A flat git graph with one lane per branch reads like the GitHub network view people will meet at work, with every commit, id and message labelled directly.

alternative.why: A flat git graph versus a 3D one: does depth help people understand branching?

assumptions: Simplified Git and GitHub: one feature branch, one pull request (#42), one reviewer
People, commit ids, messages and times are fictional; ids are short hashes, so a replayed commit gets a new id as in real Git
A conflict happens only when both sides changed the same line of the same file (here line 12 of src/dates.js)
With a merge commit or squash, the conflict is resolved by merging main into the branch; with rebase, while the branch is replayed
Rebase and merge always rewrites the feature commits, as GitHub does
units: time: playback seconds (story clock shown as day and time)
checkDescription: The commits form an acyclic graph whose parents all exist; a merge commit has two parents, rebase leaves a straight line with the feature commits replayed after the hotfix under new ids, squash adds exactly one new commit to main; a conflict appears exactly when there is a hotfix and the same file changed; and main ends up with both the hotfix and every part of the feature.

learnerPrompts.predict: Switch Merge style to Rebase. Before you press play: how many commits will main have at the end, and will any of them have two parents?
learnerPrompts.explain: Turn "Same file changed" off and then on again. Why does only one of these cases stop the merge, and what did Priya have to decide?
